answer:
Since \(5\) is prime, \(abc\) is divisible by \(5\) exactly when at least one of \(a,b,c\) is a multiple of \(5\). We can therefore count all triples with sum divisible by \(7\) and subtract those with no multiple of \(5\).

Among \(1,\ldots,99\), each residue modulo \(7\) occurs \(14\) times, with one extra number of residue \(1\). Partition these numbers into a balanced group and that extra number. Counting by how many coordinates use the extra number gives
\[
T=7^2(14^3)+3\cdot7(14^2)+3\cdot14
=138614.
\]
Here, when all coordinates come from the balanced group, any first two residues determine the third. The same reasoning applies when one or two coordinates use the extra number. Using it three times gives sum \(3\pmod7\), so contributes nothing.

After removing the multiples of \(5\), the residue counts are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
\text{Residue}&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline
\text{Count}&12&12&12&11&11&11&11
\end{array}
\]
Thus we have a balanced group with \(11\) numbers per residue, plus three extra numbers of residues \(0,1,2\). Counting by how many coordinates come from these extras gives
\[
N=7^2(11^3)+3\cdot3\cdot7(11^2)
  +3\cdot3^2\cdot11+1
=73140.
\]
The final \(1\) comes from choosing residue \(0\) in all three positions: three residues from \(\{0,1,2\}\) sum to a multiple of \(7\) only when all are zero.

Therefore, the required number of ordered triples is
\[
\boxed{138614-73140=65474}.
\]
